children: *Ipsen Has $2.3 Billion Available for Deals, CEO Says
*Ipsen Might Look for Deals to Complement Migraine Drug, CEO Says
*Potential New Ipsen Plant in U.S. Would Make Neuroscience Drugs, CEO Says
*Ipsen Is Considering Potential U.S. Manufacturing Investment, CEO Says
Ipsen Weighs U.S. Manufacturing Investment — Interview
By Adria Calatayud
France's Ipsen is considering building a production site in the U.S., joining other European drugmakers looking across the pond when planning new investments.

"Discussions are ongoing," Ipsen Chief Executive David Loew said in an interview. "No decision has been reached yet on exactly when, but this is certainly something that we are taking into consideration."
Loew said the next big plant the company builds will manufacture either its Dysport drug--a rival to AbbVie's Botox--or a next-generation medicine called corabotase that is still under development.

Many of the world's top pharmaceutical companies pledged to make multibillion-dollar investments to bring manufacturing and other operations to the U.S. over the coming years, in a bid to mitigate tariff threats by the Trump administration. In addition to big companies like AstraZeneca and Roche, smaller drugmakers like Belgium's UCB and Australia's CSL also plan to invest in new U.S. facilities.

For Ipsen, a potential U.S. plant would mark its return to manufacturing in the country. The company had production sites in Cambridge, Mass., in the past, but doesn't have any fully-owned plant in the U.S. currently. It works with multiple U.S. external manufacturers, an Ipsen spokeswoman said.
Ipsen makes Dysport--its second-biggest drug by sales--at its Wrexham site in the U.K., and has other production sites in Dublin and the French towns of Dreux and Signes.

The company is investing 130 million euros ($150.9 million) to expand production capacity in Wrexham, but this doesn't preclude or compromise the potential development of additional manufacturing in the U.S., the spokeswoman said. Exports to the U.S. from the U.K. site are exempt from tariffs under an agreement between the two countries for pharmaceuticals.

Dysport is a muscle relaxant that Ipsen markets for therapeutic indications such as a neck ailment called cervical dystonia. For cosmetic applications, the company shares rights with Switzerland's Galderma.

Ipsen earlier this year said a late-stage clinical trial showed Dysport delivered benefits in the treatment of both episodic and chronic migraine. The company previously said it aimed to launch Dysport for migraine in the second half of 2027, pending approval.
In light of the migraine-study results, Ipsen could look for complementary deals, using Dysport as an anchor product around which to build a franchise, Loew said.

"We're going to be the first company with a neurotoxin which is not just working in chronic migraine, but also in episodic migraine," he said. "It suddenly opens up another field where we're going to go and start looking at other late-stage opportunities."
After acquiring Memo Therapeutics and Kartos Therapeutics in the past two months, the company still has 2 billion euros ($2.32 billion) available for deals, Loew said.
"We can do more deals across the full spectrum," Loew said. "The goal is to have a balanced pipeline according to the stages in the clinical development, but also in terms of the therapeutic areas."

Ipsen's strategy in recent years sought to put the company on several legs so it could absorb a looming hit from generic competition for its best-selling product, cancer drug Somatuline, Loew said. Going forward, the company will pursue more deals to expand its medicine pipeline, sticking to its approach of targeting niche markets, he added.
